findings.description: If someone re-runs a stale Release run (one that was cancelled while pending, or one that failed) after a newer merge has already been released, the job counts from an older tag and publishes a second, out-of-order release for commits that are already released.
findings.body:
**A re-run of a stale Release run publishes a second, out-of-order release.**

The version comes only from the pushed commit's ancestry. `scripts/next-version.sh` runs `git describe --tags --abbrev=0 --match 'v[0-9]*.[0-9]*.[0-9]*'` on HEAD and then `git log <last>..HEAD`. `actions/checkout` puts HEAD at `GITHUB_SHA`, and a re-run keeps the original run's SHA. `fetch-depth: 0` fetches a release tag on a *later* commit, but that tag is not an ancestor of HEAD, so `describe` skips it. Nothing in the run step checks whether a newer release already covers the commit.

Stale runs are routine. With `cancel-in-progress: false`, GitHub still keeps only one *pending* run per concurrency group and cancels the older pending one when a newer run queues:

1. A is in progress. B (`fix`) is pending. C (`feat`) arrives, so B is cancelled.
2. C's run releases `v1.3.0` over B and C.
3. Someone re-runs B, which shows as cancelled. `describe` returns the tag before B, so the run publishes `v1.2.1` at B, after `v1.3.0`. B's PR is now in two releases, and the notes for `v1.2.1` are computed against the wrong previous release.

A failed run that someone re-runs after a later merge has released does the same thing. It only fails harmlessly when the computed tag name already exists.

https://github.com/AlexisBalayre/claude-code-config/blob/0f0c5c2258f07c6fc87bf52838824e3b094c9526/.github/workflows/release.yml#L37-L45
https://github.com/AlexisBalayre/claude-code-config/blob/0f0c5c2258f07c6fc87bf52838824e3b094c9526/scripts/next-version.sh#L11-L20

Suggested guard before computing `next`. It could also go in `next-version.sh` as `git tag --contains HEAD ...`, where a test could cover it:

```bash
# A release tag on this commit or a later one already covers it (a stale re-run).
if [ -n "$(git tag --contains "$GITHUB_SHA" --list 'v[0-9]*.[0-9]*.[0-9]*')" ]; then
  echo "A release already covers $GITHUB_SHA: nothing to publish."
  exit 0
fi
```

(The GitHub Actions concurrency and re-run behavior comes from documented platform behavior, not from a live run, hence medium confidence.)

findings.description: Test adequacy: no case orders a lower-level commit after a higher-level one in `git log` output, so dropping either `&& level < N` guard still passes all 15 cases.
findings.body:
**Test adequacy: the `level < 1` and `level < 2` guards are never exercised.**

`git log` lists newest first, and every case commits oldest first, so awk sees each range newest to oldest. Every existing multi-bump case reads the levels in rising order:
- `'feat: a' 'fix: b' 'docs: c'` reads docs, fix, feat.
- the bang case reads `feat: a`, then `feat(skills)!:`.

So neither guard ever has to hold a higher level against an older, lower commit:
- Removing `&& level < 1` from the fix branch leaves the suite green. The break is a newest `feat:` above an older `fix:`, which publishes a patch instead of a minor.
- Removing `&& level < 2` from the feat branch leaves the suite green. The break is a newest breaking commit above an older `feat:`, which publishes a minor instead of a major.

https://github.com/AlexisBalayre/claude-code-config/blob/0f0c5c2258f07c6fc87bf52838824e3b094c9526/scripts/next-version.sh#L23-L24

Cases to add to `tests/scripts/next-version.test.sh`. In each, the lower bump is the *older* commit. The footer needs real newlines, as in the existing footer case:

```bash
expect v1.2.0 'an older fix does not lower a newer feat' v1.1.0 'fix: a' 'feat: b'
expect v2.0.0 'an older feat does not lower a newer breaking commit' v1.1.0 'feat: a' 'fix: b

BREAKING CHANGE: x'
```

findings.description: Test adequacy: `BREAKING[ -]CHANGE:` is only tested with the space form, and a bang on a scoped non-feat type (`fix(x)!:`) is untested, so tightening either regex to the space form or to no scope passes the suite.
findings.body:
**Test adequacy: the `BREAKING-CHANGE:` (hyphen) footer form is untested.**

The script deliberately accepts both `BREAKING CHANGE:` and `BREAKING-CHANGE:` (`/^BREAKING[ -]CHANGE:/`). The only footer case uses the space form. Narrowing the regex to `^BREAKING CHANGE:` keeps the whole suite green, and then a hyphen-footer commit would ship as a patch or minor instead of a major.

The scoped-bang half of this description does not hold. Dropping the scope group from the bang regex *is* caught: `feat(skills)!: drop a skill` would then fall through to `feat` and print `v1.5.0` instead of `v2.0.0`. Only the hyphen form needs a case.

https://github.com/AlexisBalayre/claude-code-config/blob/0f0c5c2258f07c6fc87bf52838824e3b094c9526/scripts/next-version.sh#L27

Case to add to `tests/scripts/next-version.test.sh`:

```bash
expect v2.0.0 'a BREAKING-CHANGE footer bumps the major' v1.4.2 'fix: a

BREAKING-CHANGE: x'
```

findings.description: The comment "Queued, never cancelled: a run stopped between the tag and the release would leave a tag without notes" is wrong on two counts. With `cancel-in-progress: false`, a pending run is still cancelled when a newer run joins the group. And `gh release create --target` makes the tag and the release in one API call (the generate-notes request before it creates nothing), so a cancelled run cannot leave a tag without a release. Nothing is lost in practice, because the newest pending run's range takes in the cancelled run's commits. But the comment presents a routine "cancelled" status as something that never happens, which is what invites the stale re-run in Finding 1.

The table says only docs, chore, test and refactor release nothing, but the script also releases nothing for ci, build, style and revert commits, for GitHub's `Revert "feat: ..."` PR titles, and for any non-conventional subject. Wording such as 'anything else (docs, chore, ci, revert, ...)' would match what the script does; the workflow's echo text is already accurate.

The header's last mapping line, `scripts/next-version.sh   ->  v1.2.0   (.github/workflows/release.yml)`, sits inside the same arrow list as the bump rules. It reads as a fourth rule, not a usage example. Its `v1.2.0` is only true for this branch's current history, and the caller is already named in the PR body and the workflow. Move it to a separate line or drop it.

The `expect v1.1.1 'a tag that is not a release is skipped' … && { … }` case's `expect` half runs before the `nightly` tag exists, so it only repeats the 'fix bumps the patch' case; only the trailing block exercises the `--match` filter. Keep just a standalone block that builds the repo, tags `nightly` and asserts (about -2 lines).
The 'a merge subject' case runs the same no-match, no-output path as the 'docs, chore, test and refactor release nothing' and 'feature: not a type' cases, so it adds no coverage (-1 line).

No test exercises the workflow's run step (the empty-output guard and the `gh release create --target "$GITHUB_SHA"` call), and it has not run live; a fake `gh` on PATH could pin both, though for two lines of shell the cost may exceed the value.
